```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

This document is the R counterpart of the Python notebook
[Part 04 - Threads Engagement and Diffusion](../../Notebooks/Part%2004%20-%20Threads%20Engagement%20and%20Diffusion/Part%2004%20-%20Threads%20Engagement%20and%20Diffusion.ipynb).
It reconstructs a reply *cascade* from `app.bsky.feed.getPostThread`,
measures its shape with [igraph](https://r.igraph.org/), traces who
liked, reposted, and quoted the post and when, and shows that engagement
across posts is radically unequal.

How does content spread through a social network? When you post
something, some people reply, some like it, some repost it to their own
followers, and some quote it into a new conversation. Each of those
reactions can trigger further reactions, and the result is a *cascade*:
a tree of activity growing out of a single **root** post, the post that
started it all. On Bluesky, the chain of replies attached to a post is
called a **thread**, and because every reply names exactly one
**parent** (the specific post it answers), a thread naturally forms a
tree. Cascades are the basic unit of analysis for studying *information
diffusion*: questions like "do messages spread through a few big
broadcasts or long person-to-person chains?" (Goel, Anderson, Hofman, &
Watts [2016](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2015.2158)) and "does false
news travel farther and faster than true news?" (Vosoughi, Roy, & Aral
[2018](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aap9559)).

Most of what we know about online diffusion comes from Twitter, where
researchers needed special access (the "firehose" or expensive data
grants) to see complete cascades, and public APIs returned only samples.
Bluesky is different in a useful way: **every like, repost, reply, and
quote is a public record** on the AT Protocol. Anyone can ask who liked
a post and when, who amplified it, and what the entire conversation
beneath it looks like, with no special access. That makes Bluesky an
unusually open environment for replicating (and stress-testing) the
Twitter-era diffusion literature. As we will see, though, "public in
principle" does not mean "complete in one API call": the AppView prunes
its view of very large threads, and being honest about that coverage is
part of doing this well.

If cascades are new to you, Chapter 19 ("Cascading Behavior in
Networks") of Easley & Kleinberg's *[Networks, Crowds, and
Markets](https://www.cs.cornell.edu/home/kleinber/networks-book/)*, a
standard undergraduate textbook that is free online, is an accessible
companion: it explains *why* network structure makes some things spread
and others fizzle, where this document measures *how* real spreading
events actually looked.

### Learning objectives

By the end of this document you will be able to:

1. Retrieve a post's full reply thread, likes, reposts, and quotes from
   the Bluesky API.
2. Recursively parse the API's nested thread views into an igraph reply
   tree, handling deleted and blocked posts gracefully.
3. Compute cascade metrics (size, depth, breadth, and **structural
   virality**) and explain what they reveal about broadcast versus viral
   spread.
4. Analyze *when* engagement arrives (the burst-then-decay signature)
   and *who* engages in multiple ways.
5. Plot heavy-tailed engagement distributions with histograms and
   log-log CCDFs.
6. Recognize the research-design trap of sampling cascades on their
   success: "selection on the dependent variable."

## Setup

```{r libraries}
library(bskyr)
library(tidyverse)
library(jsonlite)
library(lubridate)
library(igraph)
library(patchwork)   # places ggplot figures side by side
```

As in every part of this series, the shared helper `bsky_client.R` looks
for credentials (an `atproto.json` file or bskyr's environment
variables), authenticates if it finds them, and sets `bsky_authed`. The
`knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = bsky_authed)` line then makes that flag the
default for the whole document: with credentials every chunk runs;
without them the document still knits, but the API chunks are skipped.

```{r connect}
source("bsky_client.R")
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = bsky_authed)

COLLECTED_AT <- format(now("UTC"), "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ")
```

### Collection parameters

Every cap in this part lives in one place, so you can see the whole
request budget at a glance. Each value mirrors the Python notebook (the
comment names the Python cell or `cascades.py` default it matches), so
both implementations collect the same amount of data:

```{r params}
FEED_ITEMS          <- 100   # Python: get_author_feed(actor='bsky.app', limit=100)
THREAD_FIRST_DEPTH  <- 2     # Python: the first getPostThread call, depth = 2
THREAD_DEPTH        <- 6     # Python: fetch_thread_graph(depth = 6)
THREAD_MAX_REQUESTS <- 40    # Python: fetch_thread_graph(max_requests = 40)
LIKES_CAP           <- 3500  # Python: fetch_likes(max_pages = 35), 100 per page
REPOSTS_CAP         <- 500   # Python: fetch_reposters(max_pages = 5), 100 per page
QUOTES_CAP          <- 100   # Python: fetch_quotes(max_pages = 2), 50 per page
NYT_FEED_ITEMS      <- 200   # Python: fetch_author_posts(client, 'nytimes.com', max_posts=200)
```

### A note on parsing, and a platform in flux

Bluesky changes faster than the libraries that describe it. Two kinds
of change matter. A **new type** can appear where several are allowed:
an embed can be an image set, a link card, a quote, a video, and
Bluesky keeps adding kinds (a multi-photo *gallery* embed arrived in
2026). And the **shape** of a response can change: a field gets renamed,
goes missing, or changes type.

The Python notebook shows how a *typed* client reacts, using a saved
fixture: two real `bsky.app` posts from `getAuthorFeed`, altered on
purpose so that the first carries a made-up embed type
(`app.bsky.embed.hologram#view`) and the second has its required
`indexedAt` field renamed. Python's SDK validates every response against
the models it ships with, so the renamed field raises an error (and older
SDK versions also crashed on the unknown embed).

R reads the same fixture file from the Python part's `data/` folder.
`clean = FALSE` and `jsonlite` hand us plain nested lists, and lists
validate nothing, so neither change can crash us. That is not the same as
being safe. Watch what happens when we read the field the second post
renamed:

```{r drift-fixture, eval = TRUE}
fixture <- fromJSON(
  "../../Notebooks/Part 04 - Threads Engagement and Diffusion/data/drift_fixture.json",
  simplifyVector = FALSE)

map(fixture$feed, \(item) tibble(
  embed_type = item$post$embed$`$type` %||% NA_character_,
  indexed_at = item$post$indexedAt %||% NA_character_,
  text = substr(item$post$record$text, 1, 40)
)) |> list_rbind()
```

Both posts load, the unknown embed type is just a string, and the
renamed field silently becomes `NA`. A typed client fails loudly; raw
lists fail **quietly**, and a quiet failure is the more dangerous kind,
because the analysis keeps running on missing values. That is why the
shared helpers in `bsky_client.R` (`is_repost()`, `is_reply()`) stop
with an error when the columns they expect are missing, and why it pays
to check for unexpected `NA`s after every collection.

Parsing drift is only one way a platform in flux breaks research code.
In 2026 Bluesky's moderation service stopped accepting the wildcard
label queries its API reference still documents (Part 09): the request
itself began returning HTTP 400. The defenses are the same in every
case: record your package versions along with your collection dates
(`packageVersion("bskyr")`), keep raw data you can re-parse, and treat
a refusal or an unexpected `NA` as a problem to investigate rather than
as an empty result. For deeply nested responses like threads, this part
works with raw lists and `purrr`.

## 1. Finding a study post

Diffusion analysis starts from a root post. Rather than hand-picking a
famous one, we pull the ~100 most recent feed items from the official
`bsky.app` account (9+ million followers, so its posts reliably attract
engagement) with
[`bs_get_author_feed()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_author_feed.html),
the R wrapper for
[`app.bsky.feed.getAuthorFeed`](https://endpoints.bsky.app/#bluesky-app/tag/appbskyfeed/GET/xrpc/app.bsky.feed.getAuthorFeed),
and choose a case study from the data. The author feed mixes three kinds
of items, which we need to tell apart:

* **reposts** of other accounts' posts;
* **replies** the account wrote into other threads;
* **original posts**, the roots of their own cascades, which is what we
  want.

Every post carries four engagement counters maintained by the AppView:
`reply_count`, `like_count`, `repost_count`, and `quote_count`. Here
they are for the newest item in the feed. (The counters are live, so the
numbers you see will differ from any printed copy of this document: that
is expected, not an error.)

```{r find-post}
feed <- bs_get_author_feed("bsky.app", limit = FEED_ITEMS)

feed |>
  mutate(created_at = post_created_at(feed)) |>
  select(uri, created_at, reply_count, like_count, repost_count, quote_count) |>
  head(1)
```

The endpoint also accepts a `filter` (`posts_no_replies`,
`posts_with_media`, `posts_with_video`, `posts_and_author_threads`) and
an `includePins` flag, but none of them does our filtering for us: even
`posts_no_replies` still includes reposts and the account's replies
within its own threads. (bskyr's `bs_get_author_feed()` doesn't expose
the filter anyway.) So we classify items ourselves with the
`is_repost()` and `is_reply()` helpers from `bsky_client.R`, and let
`summary()` describe each counter. Watch the gulf between the median and
the maximum:

```{r originals}
originals <- feed |>
  filter(!is_repost(feed), !is_reply(feed)) |>
  mutate(text = map_chr(record, "text", .default = ""))

c(feed_items = nrow(feed), original_posts = nrow(originals))

originals |>
  select(reply_count, like_count, repost_count, quote_count) |>
  summary()
```

Already at this account-level view the engagement counts are wildly
unequal: the medians sit far below the maxima. We will come back to that
shape in Section 5. For now, rank the originals by reply count (replies
are what build a *conversation tree*) and adopt the most-replied post as
our **case-study post**. Because it is chosen from live data, *which*
post wins, and every number computed from it below, will differ each
time the document is knitted. That is deliberate: the method is the
tutorial, not the particular numbers.

```{r case-study}
case_study <- originals |> slice_max(reply_count, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)

case_study |> select(uri, reply_count, like_count, repost_count, quote_count, text)
```

## 2. From thread views to reply trees

[`bs_get_post_thread()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_post_thread.html)
(the R wrapper for
[`app.bsky.feed.getPostThread`](https://endpoints.bsky.app/#bluesky-app/tag/appbskyfeed/GET/xrpc/app.bsky.feed.getPostThread))
returns the post and its replies nested `depth` levels down. Two words
to keep straight: a reply's **parent** is the single post it directly
answers, while the **root** is the post at the very top of the thread. A
reply deep in a conversation has a parent that is itself a reply, but
every post in the thread shares the same root. Not every node is
readable: a deleted reply comes back as a `notFoundPost` stub, and one
whose author has blocked the viewer (or been blocked) as a
`blockedPost`, both with no `post` or `replies` to traverse. We start, as the Python notebook does, with a shallow
request (`THREAD_FIRST_DEPTH`, two levels), so that truncation is easy
to see. With `clean = FALSE` the response is the API's JSON as a
plain list: `response[["thread"]]` is the root node, and each node's
`$replies` elements contain their own `$replies` — a recursive
structure, which calls for a *recursive function*: one that
handles a single node (build its row) and then calls itself on each of
that node's children. Two idioms to note: `%||%` means "use the left
side unless it is NULL, then use the right side" (our defense against
missing fields), and a node without a `$post` is the stub left behind by
a deleted or blocked reply — we record nothing for it, but its existence
is a data-quality fact worth remembering:

```{r thread-to-edges}
thread_to_edges <- function(node, parent_uri = NA_character_) {
  post <- node$post
  if (is.null(post)) {
    # a notFoundPost or blockedPost stub: the hole a deletion leaves
    return(tibble(uri = character(0)))
  }
  row <- tibble(
    uri = post$uri,
    parent_uri = parent_uri,
    author_did = post$author$did,
    created_at = post$record$createdAt %||% NA_character_,
    reply_count = post$replyCount %||% 0L,
    like_count = post$likeCount %||% 0L,
    truncated = (post$replyCount %||% 0L) > 0 && length(node$replies) == 0
  )
  children <- map(node$replies, thread_to_edges, parent_uri = post$uri)
  bind_rows(row, children)
}

response <- bs_get_post_thread(case_study$uri, depth = THREAD_FIRST_DEPTH, clean = FALSE)
root <- response[["thread"]]
tree <- thread_to_edges(root)

c(root_reply_count = root$post$replyCount,
  top_level_replies_returned = length(root$replies),
  posts = nrow(tree),
  truncated_branches = sum(tree$truncated))
```

Before going further, walk the nested structure by hand once: take the
first entry in the root's `replies` list and look at *its* `replies`. It
has exactly the same shape one level down, and that self-similarity is
why a recursive parser is the natural tool:

```{r walk-by-hand}
first_reply <- root$replies[[1]]

c(replied_at = first_reply$post$record$createdAt,
  likes = first_reply$post$likeCount,
  its_replies = length(first_reply$replies))
```

Notice the gap between the root's `reply_count` and the number of
replies actually returned: the AppView serves a **pruned view** of busy
threads. It is built to render a conversation screen, not to enumerate a
dataset. Keep that in mind; we will quantify it in a moment.

A single request only reaches `depth` levels, so deep conversations get
*truncated*: nodes that claim replies we have not seen. (The full fetch
below asks for `THREAD_DEPTH` levels per request.) The fetcher
below behaves like a small crawler doing **breadth-first search (BFS)**,
the classic traversal that explores a tree level by level: it keeps a
**frontier** (a queue of truncated nodes still to expand) and works
through it with follow-up requests until the frontier is empty or the
request budget runs out. The budget matters twice over: it keeps us
polite to the API, and it makes the collection's cost predictable before
we start. The `seen` vector prevents
double-counting posts that appear in overlapping responses:

```{r fetch-full-tree}
fetch_thread_tree <- function(uri, depth = THREAD_DEPTH, max_requests = THREAD_MAX_REQUESTS) {
  requests <- 0
  frontier <- uri
  seen <- character(0)
  pieces <- list()
  while (length(frontier) > 0 && requests < max_requests) {
    target <- frontier[[1]]
    frontier <- frontier[-1]
    response <- tryCatch(
      bs_get_post_thread(target, depth = depth, clean = FALSE),
      error = function(e) NULL
    )
    requests <- requests + 1
    Sys.sleep(0.1)
    if (is.null(response)) next
    piece <- thread_to_edges(response[["thread"]])
    piece <- filter(piece, !uri %in% seen)
    seen <- c(seen, piece$uri)
    pieces <- c(pieces, list(piece))
    frontier <- c(frontier, piece$uri[piece$truncated])
  }
  out <- bind_rows(pieces)
  attr(out, "requests_made") <- requests
  attr(out, "frontier_remaining") <- length(frontier)
  out
}

tree <- fetch_thread_tree(case_study$uri)

c(posts = nrow(tree),
  requests = attr(tree, "requests_made"),
  unexpanded = attr(tree, "frontier_remaining"))
```

### How much of the cascade did we get?

Every node reports how many direct replies it has, so we can compare
the replies *promised* by those counters with the reply edges we
actually *retrieved*. For quiet threads the two match; for a mega-thread
the AppView's pruning means we have a sample of the cascade, biased
toward whatever the server chose to surface (it does not document its
ranking):

```{r coverage}
promised <- sum(tree$reply_count)
retrieved <- sum(!is.na(tree$parent_uri))

c(promised = promised, retrieved = retrieved,
  coverage = round(retrieved / promised, 3))
```

Do not be alarmed if that coverage is low: on a mega-thread with tens of
thousands of promised replies it can land in the low single digits of a
percent. The crawler is working correctly. The AppView caps how many
replies it returns *per node* (a breadth cut), and no amount of
re-querying recovers replies the server declines to list. The protocol's
promise still holds (every reply is a public record in its author's
repository, and Part 10's firehose-based collection can capture
cascades completely), but the convenient endpoint alone does not
deliver it for threads this size. The honest move is the one we just
made: report coverage next to the metrics.

## 3. Cascade metrics

The diffusion literature summarizes a cascade's shape with a few
standard numbers. In tree vocabulary, *depth* is vertical (how far a
node sits from the root) and *breadth* is horizontal (how many nodes
share a level):

* **size**: how many posts the tree contains;
* **max depth**: the longest chain of replies-to-replies;
* **mean depth**: how far from the root the average reply sits;
* **max breadth**: the largest number of posts at any single level;
* **structural virality**: the average distance between *all pairs* of
  posts in the (undirected) tree (Goel et al.
  [2016](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2015.2158)).

Structural virality is the interesting one. Size alone cannot
distinguish a celebrity's post that ten thousand people answer directly
(a *broadcast*) from a chain letter passed person to person ten thousand
times (*viral* spread): both are size 10,001. Average pairwise distance
can: in the star every pair of leaves is 2 hops apart, while in the
chain typical pairs are thousands of hops apart. igraph's
[`mean_distance()`](https://r.igraph.org/reference/distances.html)
computes it exactly. We build the tree as an igraph object and measure
its shape:

```{r metrics}
edges <- tree |> filter(!is.na(parent_uri)) |> select(parent_uri, uri)
Gt <- graph_from_data_frame(edges, directed = TRUE,
                            vertices = tibble(name = tree$uri))

depths <- distances(Gt, v = case_study$uri, mode = "out")[1, ]

structural_virality <- function(g) {
  mean_distance(as_undirected(g), unconnected = FALSE)
}

finite_depths <- depths[is.finite(depths)]

tibble(
  size = vcount(Gt),
  max_depth = max(finite_depths),
  mean_depth = mean(finite_depths),
  max_breadth = max(table(finite_depths)),
  unique_authors = n_distinct(tree$author_did),
  structural_virality = structural_virality(Gt)
)
```

A structural-virality value on its own is hard to judge: is the number
above broadcast-ish or viral-ish? To calibrate it, build the two extreme
trees *of the same size* with igraph's generators,
[`make_star()`](https://r.igraph.org/reference/make_star.html) (one
center connected to everyone: a pure broadcast) and a non-circular
[`make_ring()`](https://r.igraph.org/reference/make_ring.html) (a single
chain: pure person-to-person spread), and compute the same metric on
them. Our cascade has to land somewhere between those two poles:

```{r calibrate}
n <- vcount(Gt)
c(
  star_broadcast = structural_virality(make_star(n, mode = "out")),
  observed = structural_virality(Gt),
  chain_viral = structural_virality(make_ring(n, circular = FALSE))
)
```

The observed value sits between the two poles, as almost all real
cascades do, and much closer to the broadcast star than to the chain:
Goel et al. (2016) found the same across a billion Twitter events.
Because the server prunes busy threads mostly at the first level (direct
replies to the root), the true cascade is probably even more
broadcast-like than the tree we retrieved: pruning biases structural
virality *upward*.

The **depth profile**, how many posts sit at each level, shows the same
structure visually: a fat first level of direct replies that thins
quickly, with a long shallow tail of back-and-forth conversations.

```{r depth-profile, fig.width=8, fig.height=4}
tibble(depth = depths[is.finite(depths)]) |>
  count(depth) |>
  ggplot(aes(depth, n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "Depth (replies away from the root)", y = "Posts at this depth",
       title = "Depth profile of the case-study reply tree") +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Drawing the reply tree

Trees beg to be drawn. igraph's
[`layout_as_tree()`](https://r.igraph.org/reference/layout_as_tree.html)
with `circular = TRUE` computes a radial layout: each node's radius is
its depth, so every subtree occupies its own wedge. We hand those
coordinates to ggplot, which lets us color each post by its depth and
add a colorbar. The red point is the root:

```{r draw-tree, fig.width=9, fig.height=9}
layout <- layout_as_tree(Gt, root = case_study$uri, circular = TRUE)
nodes <- tibble(x = layout[, 1], y = layout[, 2],
                depth = depths, is_root = V(Gt)$name == case_study$uri)
edge_ends <- ends(Gt, E(Gt), names = FALSE)
segments <- tibble(x = layout[edge_ends[, 1], 1], y = layout[edge_ends[, 1], 2],
                   xend = layout[edge_ends[, 2], 1], yend = layout[edge_ends[, 2], 2])

ggplot() +
  geom_segment(data = segments, aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
               color = "gray", alpha = 0.4, linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_point(data = filter(nodes, !is_root), aes(x, y, color = depth), size = 1) +
  geom_point(data = filter(nodes, is_root), aes(x, y), color = "#DC143C", size = 4) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(name = "Reply depth") +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = paste0("Reply tree of the case-study post (",
                      vcount(Gt), " posts retrieved)")) +
  theme_void()
```

## 4. Who engages, and when

Replies are only one channel of engagement. Three more endpoints tell us
who reacted in lighter-weight ways:

* [`app.bsky.feed.getLikes`](https://endpoints.bsky.app/#bluesky-app/tag/appbskyfeed/GET/xrpc/app.bsky.feed.getLikes):
  who liked the post, **with timestamps**;
* [`app.bsky.feed.getRepostedBy`](https://endpoints.bsky.app/#bluesky-app/tag/appbskyfeed/GET/xrpc/app.bsky.feed.getRepostedBy):
  who amplified it to their followers (profiles only, no timestamps);
* [`app.bsky.feed.getQuotes`](https://endpoints.bsky.app/#bluesky-app/tag/appbskyfeed/GET/xrpc/app.bsky.feed.getQuotes):
  quote posts that embed it, each the root of a potential new cascade.

It is worth pausing on what a quietly unusual dataset the like list is:
on most platforms, *who* liked *what*, *when* is private or paywalled,
while on Bluesky each like is a public record. Likes carry two
timestamps, `createdAt` from the liker's client and `indexedAt` from the
network, which lets us reconstruct the post's attention curve. With
`clean = FALSE`, [`bs_get_post_likes()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_post_likes.html) hands back a list of raw response
pages; each page has a `$likes` list whose elements we flatten into one
row apiece, then convert "when was this like indexed" into "hours since
the post was born".

Which timestamp should we trust? `createdAt` is written by the liker's
own client, and client clocks can be minutes or years off, so a few
likes appear to predate the post they like. We count those, as a data
quality check, but don't use them. `indexedAt` is stamped by the
network's server, which makes it the defensible choice for timing; even
so, a like *indexed* before the post existed is impossible, so we drop
and report any such rows rather than let them distort the timeline:

```{r likes}
likes_raw <- bs_get_post_likes(case_study$uri, limit = LIKES_CAP, clean = FALSE)

likes <- map(likes_raw, \(page) {
  map(page$likes, \(l) tibble(
    did = l$actor$did,
    handle = l$actor$handle,
    created_at = l$createdAt,
    indexed_at = l$indexedAt
  )) |> list_rbind()
}) |> list_rbind()

post_time <- ymd_hms(case_study$record[[1]]$created_at, quiet = TRUE)

likes <- likes |>
  mutate(
    created_at = ymd_hms(created_at, quiet = TRUE),
    indexed_at = ymd_hms(indexed_at, quiet = TRUE),
    hours_since_post = as.numeric(difftime(indexed_at, post_time,
                                           units = "hours"))
  )

clock_skew <- sum(likes$created_at < post_time, na.rm = TRUE)
impossible <- sum(likes$hours_since_post < 0, na.rm = TRUE)

likes <- likes |>
  filter(hours_since_post >= 0) |>
  arrange(hours_since_post)

c(likes_retrieved = nrow(likes) + impossible,
  reported_at_collection = case_study$like_count,
  client_clock_predates_post = clock_skew,
  indexed_before_post_dropped = impossible)
```

Compare the likes retrieved with the count the post reported. Withdrawn
likes and deleted accounts explain a small gap. A large gap, even when
we stayed under `LIKES_CAP`, means the endpoint stopped returning pages
early: the like list is a sample, not a census, and everything we
compute from it inherits that.

### The burst, then the decay

Attention on social media is front-loaded: a post earns most of its
engagement in the first hours while feeds and notifications surface it,
then decays to a trickle. Plotting cumulative likes against time since
posting makes that signature visible (a steep initial rise that bends
toward a plateau), and the per-hour histogram shows the same burst
directly, often with small daily echoes as different time zones wake up.
`patchwork`'s `+` places the two plots side by side:

```{r burst, fig.width=12, fig.height=4}
cumulative_plot <- likes |>
  mutate(cumulative = row_number()) |>
  ggplot(aes(hours_since_post / 24, cumulative)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "Days since post", y = "Cumulative likes",
       title = "Cumulative likes over time") +
  theme_minimal()

burst_plot <- likes |>
  filter(hours_since_post <= 72) |>
  ggplot(aes(hours_since_post)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 72, fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "Hours since post (first 72)", y = "Likes per hour",
       title = "The initial burst") +
  theme_minimal()

cumulative_plot + burst_plot
```

### Reposters and quoters

Reposts are the engine of diffusion (they place the post in *new*
audiences' feeds) and quotes start new conversations about it.
[`bs_get_reposts()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_reposts.html)
lists who amplified the post, and
[`bs_get_quotes()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_quotes.html)
lists posts that embed it. Note the affordance gap in the API: likes
come with timestamps, reposts do not (a reposter row is just a profile),
so timing analyses of amplification need different collection
strategies (Part 10's firehose records repost events as they happen).
Both lists are capped by the parameters at the top of the document:

```{r reposts-quotes}
reposters <- bs_get_reposts(case_study$uri, limit = REPOSTS_CAP)
quotes <- bs_get_quotes(case_study$uri, limit = QUOTES_CAP)

c(reposters_retrieved = nrow(reposters),
  reposts_reported = case_study$repost_count,
  quotes_retrieved = nrow(quotes),
  quotes_reported = case_study$quote_count,
  likes_on_quote_posts = sum(quotes$like_count, na.rm = TRUE),
  replies_to_quote_posts = sum(quotes$reply_count, na.rm = TRUE))
```

The quote posts earn engagement of their own: each one can seed its own
cascade, so diffusion on Bluesky is a forest, not a single tree.

### Do the same people like and repost?

```{r overlap}
both <- intersect(likes$did, reposters$did)

c(likers = n_distinct(likes$did),
  reposters = n_distinct(reposters$did),
  both = length(both),
  share_of_reposters_who_liked = round(length(both) / nrow(reposters), 2),
  share_of_likers_who_reposted = round(length(both) / n_distinct(likes$did), 3))
```

Read the two shares against each other. Only a small fraction of likers
go on to repost: engagement behaves like a funnel from cheap signals to
costly ones. The other direction varies more from post to post: most
reposters of a product announcement also like it, but a post people
share to argue with can draw many reposts without likes. And if the like
list is incomplete (see the shortfall above), the overlap is undercounted.

## 5. Heavy-tailed engagement across posts

Step back from one cascade to the *distribution* of engagement across
many posts. Engagement is famously **heavy-tailed**. A distribution has
a *heavy tail* when extreme values are common enough to dominate the
totals: unlike human heights, where nobody is fifty feet tall, post
engagement routinely produces values hundreds or thousands of times the
median. Most posts receive little attention while a few receive enormous
amounts, and the "average post" is a misleading fiction (Bakshy, Hofman,
Mason, & Watts 2011 found the same for cascade sizes seeded by ordinary
Twitter users).

For contrast with `bsky.app`'s megaphone, we also collect ~200 recent
feed items from `nytimes.com`, The New York Times, a newsroom that posts
dozens of times a day to over a million followers:

```{r nyt-feed}
nyt_feed <- bs_get_author_feed("nytimes.com", limit = NYT_FEED_ITEMS)
nyt_originals <- nyt_feed |>
  filter(!is_repost(nyt_feed), !is_reply(nyt_feed))

c(feed_items = nrow(nyt_feed), original_posts = nrow(nyt_originals))

nyt_originals |>
  select(reply_count, like_count, repost_count, quote_count) |>
  summary()
```

A linear-scale histogram mostly shows one tall bar near zero and a few
invisible outliers: the tail is exactly what it hides. The standard fix
is the **complementary cumulative distribution function (CCDF)** on
log-log axes: for each engagement level *x*, plot the fraction of posts
with *at least* *x*. Heavy-tailed distributions decay slowly, roughly
straight on log-log axes, while thin-tailed ones plunge. Zero-count
posts are dropped, since log 0 is undefined. The two views side by side:

```{r heavy-tails, fig.width=12, fig.height=4.5}
ccdf <- function(x) {
  x <- sort(x[!is.na(x)])
  tibble(value = x, p = 1 - (seq_along(x) - 1) / length(x))
}

linear_plot <- ggplot(originals, aes(like_count)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "Likes per post", y = "Posts",
       title = "@bsky.app like counts (linear scale)") +
  theme_minimal()

ccdf_plot <- bind_rows(
  ccdf(originals$like_count) |> mutate(account = "bsky.app"),
  ccdf(nyt_originals$like_count) |> mutate(account = "nytimes.com")
) |>
  filter(value > 0) |>
  ggplot(aes(value, p, color = account)) +
  geom_step() +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("bsky.app" = "steelblue", "nytimes.com" = "darkorange")) +
  labs(x = "Likes per post", y = "P(X ≥ x)",
       title = "Like-count CCDF (log-log)") +
  theme_minimal()

linear_plot + ccdf_plot
```

One number can summarize the same inequality: what share of *all* likes
went to the top 10% of posts? If attention were spread evenly the answer
would be 10%; heavy tails push it far higher, the "winner-take-most"
signature you will meet again in every engagement dataset you collect:

```{r top10-share}
bind_rows(
  mutate(originals, account = "bsky.app"),
  mutate(nyt_originals, account = "nytimes.com")
) |>
  group_by(account) |>
  summarise(
    median_likes = median(like_count, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_likes = max(like_count, na.rm = TRUE),
    top10pct_share = {
      l <- sort(like_count, decreasing = TRUE)
      sum(head(l, ceiling(length(l) * .1))) / max(sum(l), 1)
    }
  )
```

Both accounts show the heavy-tailed signature (engagement inequality is
a property of the *medium*, not just of celebrity), but the curves sit
far apart on the x-axis (compare the two medians above), even though
both accounts count their followers in the millions. The gap is about
*posting style*, not audience size: `bsky.app` posts rarely, and each
announcement lands on the whole audience at once, while a newsroom
floods the zone with dozens of posts a day, diluting attention across
them. Follower count is **potential** reach; engagement per post is what
the audience actually does with it. And when an account's occasional
post does break out, the extra reach comes from reposts rippling
outward, the **viral** pathway. Goel et al. (2016) showed that broadcast
and viral diffusion are genuinely different mechanisms that produce
cascades of similar size with very different shapes, which is precisely
why structural virality (Section 3) was invented: size alone cannot tell
you *how* something spread.

## 6. Saving the data

We save two artifacts to `data/` for reuse:

* **`engagement_summary.csv`**: per-post engagement counts for both
  accounts. We keep post URIs (they identify the *posts*, which we
  analyze) but drop the text: it is re-fetchable from the URI, and there
  is no reason to redistribute it.
* **`case_study_likes.csv`**: the timing of likes on the case-study
  post, with **timestamps and an anonymous index only**.

That second choice is *data minimization* in action. Our research
question (when does engagement arrive?) needs timestamps, not
identities. The liker DIDs are public records, and keeping them would be
defensible for a question that genuinely requires them, but a saved file
should carry the minimum needed for its purpose: files get copied,
shared, and forgotten, and a de-identified file of timestamps cannot
become a list of *who liked what* in someone else's hands. The last line
lists what the collection left on disk; keeping `data/` small enforces
the same discipline.

```{r save}
dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)

bind_rows(
  mutate(originals, account = "bsky.app"),
  mutate(nyt_originals, account = "nytimes.com")
) |>
  select(account, uri, reply_count, like_count,
         repost_count, quote_count) |>
  mutate(collected_at = COLLECTED_AT) |>
  write_csv("data/engagement_summary.csv")

likes |>
  transmute(liker_index = row_number(),   # anonymous index, not an identity
            hours_since_post, collected_at = COLLECTED_AT) |>
  write_csv("data/case_study_likes.csv")

files <- list.files("data", full.names = TRUE)
tibble(file = files, size_kb = round(file.size(files) / 1024))
```

## 7. Research design: studying diffusion without sampling on success

The methods above are straightforward; the design decisions around them
are where diffusion studies succeed or fail.

### Selection on the dependent variable

The most tempting way to study virality is to collect viral things:
scrape the trending page, search for posts with thousands of reposts,
ask "what do hit posts have in common?" This is **sampling on the
dependent variable**, and it cannot answer the question. Whatever the
hits have in common (emotional language, images, posting time),
countless *failed* posts shared those traits too; without the failures
in your sample, you cannot tell features that cause spread from features
that are merely common. The diffusion literature's central empirical
fact makes this acute: cascades' size distribution is so heavy-tailed
that the typical post spawns *no* cascade at all (Goel, Watts, &
Goldstein 2012). A sample of successes is a sample of extreme outliers.

The defensible design samples posts **at the starting line, before their
outcomes are known**, then follows every cascade, including the
overwhelmingly common tiny ones. This document did that only halfway,
and it is worth being precise about which half:

* The **engagement distributions** in Section 5 are success-blind. They
  use each account's most recent posts, a time-window frame chosen before
  looking at engagement, so the low-engagement posts in
  `engagement_summary.csv` are data, not noise.
* The **case-study cascade** in Sections 2–4 is not. We picked it
  *because* it had the most replies of `bsky.app`'s recent posts, which
  is sampling on the dependent variable in miniature. Its size, depth and
  structural virality describe an outlier chosen for being large, and
  they tell us nothing about how a typical Bluesky post spreads. That was
  a fine choice for teaching the methods (a big tree has something to
  measure) and the wrong one for a finding.

A success-blind version of Section 3 would compute the same cascade
metrics for *every* post in the time window, small and large alike;
Exercise 4 is a step in that direction, and the first research project
below is the full design. At platform scale, the same logic means
sampling from the firehose (Part 10) or from a pre-registered panel of
accounts (Part 01), as Bakshy et al. (2011) did when they followed all
74 million diffusion events from 1.6 million seeds (successes and
failures alike) to ask whether "influencers" were worth their price.

### Conditioning on content: the true-versus-false-news design

The marquee Twitter diffusion study, Vosoughi, Roy, & Aral
([2018](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aap9559)), shows the other
defensible move: condition on a *pre-treatment* property of content
rather than on its success. They started from claims independently
fact-checked as true or false, collected **every** cascade spreading each
claim (~126,000 cascades), and compared the distributions: falsehood
spread farther, faster, deeper, and more broadly, and the false cascades
were more *viral* in the structural sense of Section 3. Every
measurement in that paper (cascade size, depth, breadth, structural
virality, timing curves) is one you can now compute from public Bluesky
data. The replication question writes itself: do their findings hold on
a platform with different curation, no engagement-optimizing algorithm
in the default feed, and a different population?

### Bluesky-specific cautions

Three things to carry from this document into any such design: the
AppView prunes very large threads, so condition your collection plan
(thread endpoint vs. firehose) on the cascade sizes you expect;
engagement counters are *live* (they were different yesterday and will
be different tomorrow), so record collection times; and deleted replies
(`notFoundPost`) mean retrospective collection systematically misses the
most ephemeral parts of conversations.

## Ethics and limitations

**Third parties everywhere.** We chose `bsky.app`, an institutional
account, as our root, but the people in its reply tree, like list, and
repost list are ordinary users who never opted into being studied.
Cascade data is *inherently* about third parties. This document's
defaults are worth keeping: identify institutional accounts, aggregate
over individuals (depth profiles, overlap rates, distributions) rather
than spotlighting them, and avoid quoting strangers' replies verbatim (a
verbatim post is trivially re-identifiable through search even if you
withhold the handle). That is also why the hand-walk in Section 2 prints
the first reply's timing and counts but not its author.

**Public is not consented.** Likes are public records on the AT
Protocol, but most users have not read the protocol docs, and many would
be surprised that *who liked what, when* is globally queryable (Fiesler
& Proferes 2018 found exactly this surprise among Twitter users). That a
field is available is the beginning of the ethical analysis, not the
end. We saved like *timings* without identities because our question
needed nothing more; "public data" also does not automatically mean
IRB-exempt, so ask, and consult the AoIR guidelines (franzke et al.
2020).

**Deletion and withdrawal.** The `notFoundPost` stubs we skipped are
people exercising the right to take things back. Saved archives should
record collection dates (ours do) and honor deletions when data is
shared or re-published.

**Limitations of the measurements.** Our case study was chosen for its
size (Section 7), so its metrics describe an outlier, and its tree is a
*pruned sample* of a very large thread: coverage was quantified in
Section 2, the server's selection rule is undocumented, and metrics like
breadth and structural virality inherit that bias. Engagement counts
condition on visible reactions: Bluesky exposes no impression counts, so
we observe who *acted*, never who *saw* and scrolled past ("engagement"
is not "exposure"). All counts are live and change between knits of this
document. And Bluesky's population skews toward early adopters and
Twitter migrants, so prevalence estimates do not generalize to "the
public", just as Twitter's never did. The platform's structural
differences (no engagement-ranked default feed, composable moderation)
are part of what makes replication here scientifically interesting
rather than merely convenient.

## Exercises

These extend the document in roughly increasing order of effort. For all
of them, keep the politeness habits: small request budgets, sleeps
between calls, and recorded collection times.

1. **A different case study.** Re-run Sections 2–4 with the
   *second*-most-replied post (`originals |> arrange(desc(reply_count)) |> slice(2)`),
   or with the most-replied original post from another large account
   (try `npr.org`). Which conclusions change qualitatively, and which are
   stable across case studies?
2. **A bigger crawl budget.** Re-collect the case-study tree with
   `fetch_thread_tree(case_study$uri, depth = 10, max_requests = 80)`.
   How much do node count, coverage, and structural virality move? Judge
   when extra requests stop paying.
3. **Ranking by repost instead of reply.** Section 1 ranked posts by
   `reply_count`. Re-rank `originals` by `repost_count` and compare the
   two top-5 lists; then compute the Spearman rank correlation among all
   four counters with `cor(..., method = "spearman")`. Are starting
   conversations and being amplified the same kind of success?
4. **Structural virality across five posts.** Loop over the five
   most-replied originals, fetch each reply tree with a modest budget
   (`max_requests = 10`), and assemble their size, depth and structural
   virality into one tibble. Does structural virality grow with size, or
   are bigger cascades just bigger stars?
5. **Tree shape versus engagement.** Using the cascades from Exercise 4,
   compute for each the fraction of retrieved posts at depth 1 (direct
   replies to the root) and plot it against the root's `like_count`. Do
   more-liked posts have flatter, more broadcast-like conversations, and
   what does AppView pruning do to your confidence in the answer?
6. **Quote posts as new roots.** Take the most-liked quote post from
   Section 4 (`quotes |> slice_max(like_count, n = 1)`) and fetch *its*
   reply tree. Compare its depth profile to the original's: does
   commentary about a post breed a different conversation shape than the
   post itself?

## Research project ideas

**1. Is Bluesky diffusion broadcast or viral? (a Goel et al. 2016
replication).** *Question:* does the joint distribution of cascade size
and structural virality on Bluesky match the broadcast-dominated picture
Goel et al. ([2016](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2015.2158)) found
across a billion Twitter events, on a platform whose default feeds are
not engagement-ranked? *Data:* a success-blind sample of root posts:
every original post from a stratified panel of a few hundred accounts
over a fixed week (the paneling logic of Part 01), so the tiny cascades
stay in the sample. *Method:* fetch each reply tree with a fixed request
budget, compute size, depth, breadth, and structural virality, and plot
virality against size as Goel et al. do. *Expected challenge:* AppView
pruning biases the metrics for large threads; either restrict claims to
the small-to-medium cascades where coverage is complete, or collect
replies prospectively from the firehose (Part 10) and treat this
document's endpoint as a validation check.

**2. Do contested claims spread differently? (a Vosoughi et al.
2018-style design).** *Question:* do posts linking to independently
fact-checked *false* claims spread farther, faster, deeper, and more
virally than posts linking to *true* ones? *Data:* a set of claim URLs
labeled true or false by fact-checking organizations; an authenticated
search collection (Part 02) of every Bluesky post carrying each URL;
then this document's four endpoints for every matching post. *Method:*
per-claim cascade collection, then compare the distributions of size,
depth, max breadth, structural virality, and like-arrival speed between
the truth categories, conditioning on a pre-treatment property of the
content, not on its success. *Expected challenge:* claim matching
(paraphrases and screenshots evade URL search, so measure your recall
on a hand-coded subsample) and Bluesky's smaller, early-adopter-skewed
population, which limits generalization but is itself part of the
comparative story.

**3. Conversation shape as an early-warning signal.** *Question:* does
the shape of a thread's first hours (depth profile, branching, the
reply-to-like ratio) predict whether it becomes sustained back-and-forth
argument (deep, narrow chains among few accounts) or fades after a
one-hop burst? *Data:* a time-window sample of fresh root posts from
accounts of varied sizes, with each thread re-crawled at fixed intervals
(1, 6, 24, and 72 hours after posting). *Method:* compute shape metrics
at each snapshot and model final depth and size from the early-snapshot
features. *Expected challenge:* repeated crawling multiplies request
volume, so budgets and sleeps matter more than ever; and deletions
accumulate over snapshots, meaning the most volatile threads are
precisely the most undercounted, a bias worth measuring and reporting.
